activities.title: Mastering System.out.printf() & Format Specifiers
activities.content:
### Why printf()?

While `print()` and `println()` work well for simple output, formatting numbers (like showing exactly 2 decimal places for money: `Rs 49.90` instead of `49.900000000000006`) becomes awkward with string concatenation.

Java provides `System.out.printf()` (print formatted):
```java
System.out.printf(formatString, arg1, arg2, ...);
```
Inside the `formatString`, you place **format specifiers** starting with `%` that act as placeholders for variables.

---

### Core Format Specifiers

| Specifier | Data Type | Example Argument | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%d` | Decimal Integer (`byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`) | `42` | `42` |
| `%f` | Floating-Point (`float`, `double`) | `3.14159` | `3.141590` (default 6 decimals) |
| `%s` | String / Object text | `"Java"` | `Java` |
| `%c` | Character (`char`) | `'A'` | `A` |
| `%b` | Boolean (`boolean`) | `true` | `true` |
| `%n` | Platform-independent Newline | *(no argument needed)* | Moves cursor to next line |

> [!NOTE]
> Unlike `println()`, `printf()` does **NOT** automatically append a newline at the end. You must explicitly include `%n` or `\n` when you want a line break!

---

### Controlling Decimal Precision (`%.Nf`)

To control how many decimal digits appear, insert `.N` before the `f`:

```java
double pi = 3.14159265;
double price = 49.9;

System.out.printf("Pi: %.2f%n", pi);       // Prints: Pi: 3.14
System.out.printf("Price: Rs %.2f%n", price); // Prints: Price: Rs 49.90
System.out.printf("Exact: %.4f%n", pi);    // Prints: Exact: 3.1416 (rounded!)
```
Notice that Java automatically rounds the last displayed digit!

---

### Column Widths & Tabular Alignment

You can specify a minimum field width by inserting an integer before the specifier:
- `%10s`: Right-aligns within a 10-character wide field (spaces padded on left).
- `%-10s`: Left-aligns within a 10-character wide field (spaces padded on right).
- `%05d`: Pads integers with leading zeros to width 5 (e.g. `00042`).

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("%-12s %5s %10s%n", "Item", "Qty", "Price");
        System.out.printf("%-12s %5d %10.2f%n", "Apples", 4, 120.50);
        System.out.printf("%-12s %5d %10.2f%n", "Notebook", 10, 450.00);
    }
}
```
**Output:**
```
Item           Qty      Price
Apples           4     120.50
Notebook        10     450.00
```

breakdown.whatIsIt: printf formats text and numbers with exact precision, column widths, and alignments.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Financial systems, invoices, tables, and reports require deterministic decimal rounding and aligned columns.
howItWorks: Placeholders begin with % followed by type indicators (%d, %f, %s, %c).
%.2f rounds floating-point numbers to exactly two decimal places.
Width flags (e.g. %15s, %-15s) align data into consistent table columns.
keyTakeaways: printf does NOT add a newline automatically; use %n at the end of the format string.
%.2f is standard for currency amounts and percentages.
Minus flag (%-10s) left-aligns text; positive (%10s) right-aligns.
Passing wrong types (e.g. %d for double) throws IllegalFormatConversionException.

questions.prompt: Which format specifier is used for formatting standard integers (int, long)?
questions.explanation: In Java printf, %d represents decimal integer (base 10 integer). %i is not supported in Java printf.

questions.prompt: What is the output of: System.out.printf("%.2f", 45.6789);?
questions.explanation: %.2f rounds to 2 decimal places. Since the third decimal digit is 8 (>= 5), 45.67 rounds up to 45.68.

questions.prompt: Does System.out.printf() automatically advance to a new line after printing?
options: No, you must explicitly include %n or \n
Only if there are more than 3 arguments
Yes, if the last specifier is %s
questions.explanation: printf does not append a newline automatically. You must append %n or \n to advance to the next line.
hints: It behaves like print(), not println().

questions.prompt: What does the format specifier %05d do to the number 42?
options: Pads 42 with 5 spaces on the left
Pads 42 with leading zeros to make total width 5: '00042'
questions.explanation: The '0' flag causes the output to be padded with leading zeros up to the minimum field width (5), yielding '00042'.
hints: The 0 after % is a padding flag.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between %s and %-10s?
options: %s prints in lowercase, %-10s prints in uppercase
%-10s left-aligns the string within a 10-character wide field, padding spaces on the right
%-10s cuts the string off after 10 characters
questions.explanation: The minus flag '-' indicates left-justification within the specified minimum width (10 characters).
hints: The '-' flag aligns text to the left.

questions.prompt: Why is %n preferred over \n inside printf format strings?
options: %n is platform-independent, outputting \r\n on Windows and \n on Unix/macOS
%n prints two blank lines instead of one
questions.explanation: %n generates the platform-specific line separator dynamically (e.g. \r\n on Windows, \n on Linux/Mac), ensuring universal compatibility.
hints: Consider how line endings differ between Windows and Linux.

questions.prompt: What happens if you execute: System.out.printf("%d", 12.34);?
options: It prints 12 by truncating the decimal
questions.explanation: Format specifiers are type-checked at runtime. %d expects an integral type; passing a floating-point double throws IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double.
hints: Format specifier types must match the argument types.

questions.explanation: Width 6 without '-' is right-aligned by default. 'Cat' is 3 characters, so 3 spaces are padded on the left: '[   Cat]'.
hints: Positive width numbers right-align by default.

questions.prompt: How do you print a literal '%' percent symbol using printf?
questions.explanation: Because '%' denotes the start of a format specifier, to print a literal percent sign you must escape it with another percent sign: '%%'.
hints: Double the symbol to escape it in printf.

practice.title: Format Product Pricing Table
practice.problemStatement:
Write a complete Java program in the Main class that prints a 2-line pricing table using printf:
Item: Coffee      | Price: $004.50
Item: Sandwich    | Price: $012.75

Requirements:
• Use %-12s for the item name.
• Use %06.2f for the price (zero-padded to width 6 with 2 decimal places).
practice.expectedOutput:
Item: Coffee       | Price: $004.50
Item: Sandwich     | Price: $012.75
hints: First item is "Coffee" with 4.5; second is "Sandwich" with 12.75.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Output Formatting

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between %n and \n in printf?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer:
`
` is a literal UNIX newline character (ASCII 10). `%n` is a platform-independent format specifier that writes the host OS line separator (`
` on Windows, `
` on Linux and macOS). `%n` is strictly supported only inside format strings, whereas `
` can be used in any string.
keyPoints: %n emits OS-dependent line breaks; \n is always literal ASCII 10.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you pass an int argument to a %f specifier?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java throws a runtime `java.util.IllegalFormatConversionException: f != java.lang.Integer`. Unlike standard arithmetic where widening happens automatically, `printf` arguments are boxed to `Object` and strictly checked against the specifier type.
keyPoints: printf arguments do not undergo automatic widening; type mismatches throw runtime exceptions.

interviewQA.question: How do you round a double to 2 decimal places using printf?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Use the `%.2f` specifier. For example: `System.out.printf("%.2f", 19.876);` prints `19.88`. Java automatically rounds the final displayed digit based on the following decimal place.
keyPoints: %.2f formats to two decimal places with standard half-up rounding.

interviewQA.question: What does String.format() do compared to System.out.printf()?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `System.out.printf()` formats text and directly prints it to the console. `String.format()` accepts the exact same format specifiers but returns the formatted text as a new `String` object without printing it. This is useful for storing formatted data in variables or building logs.
keyPoints: printf prints to console; String.format returns the formatted String for variable storage.

interviewQA.question: How do you print a literal '%' character in a formatted string?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In printf and String.format, `%` introduces a specifier. To output a literal percent sign, you must write `%%`. For example: `System.out.printf("Discount: %d%%", 15);` prints `Discount: 15%`.

interviewQA.question: How does left-alignment work in printf?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: By default, specifying a width like `%10s` right-aligns text with leading spaces. Adding the minus flag (`%-10s`) instructs the formatter to left-align the content and pad spaces on the right.
keyPoints: Minus flag (%-10s) left-aligns and pads trailing spaces.

interviewQA.question: What does the zero flag (%08d) do?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The zero flag `0` pads the integer with leading zeros instead of spaces to satisfy the specified minimum width. For instance, `System.out.printf("%05d", 7);` produces `00007`.
keyPoints: %0Nd pads numbers with leading zeros to width N.

interviewQA.question: Can you format multiple values of different types in a single printf call?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. `printf` is a varargs method (`printf(String format, Object... args)`). You can pass as many arguments as there are format specifiers in the format string, and they are matched in sequential order.
keyPoints: printf accepts variable arguments (varargs) matching specifiers left to right.

activities.title: Topic Confidence Checklist
checklist: I know the core specifiers: %d, %f, %s, %c, and %b.
I can format money and percentages to two decimal places with %.2f.
I know that printf does not add a newline automatically and I use %n.
I can align columns using positive (%10s) and negative (%-10s) widths.
I know how to escape the percent symbol using %%.
